Sample topic
The Impact of Urban Green Spaces on Community Well-Being

In this project, I will explore how urban green spaces, such as parks and community gardens, contribute to the overall well-being of city residents (Jennings et al., 2024). I plan to investigate the psychological and physical health benefits associated with access to these green areas, including reduced stress levels, increased physical activity, and improved social cohesion among community members (Lampert et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2025). By analyzing peer-reviewed studies and case examples from cities that have successfully integrated green spaces into their urban planning, I aim to demonstrate the importance of prioritizing green infrastructure in sustainable city development. This topic not only highlights the environmental aspect of sustainability but also emphasizes its social implications, making it a compelling area of research.

Introduction

Is food a sustainability/environmental issue?

Introduction

How should we approach sustainable food systems?

The omnivore’s dilemma: when we can eat almost anything, what should we eat? To find out, Pollan follows four meals back to where they came from, and each one tells the story of a different food system.

  1. 1
    Industrial

    A fast-food meal, traced back to Iowa cornfields and a Kansas feedlot. Corn, grown with synthetic fertilizer, feeds the cattle and fills processed food.

  2. 2
    Industrial organic

    A Whole Foods meal: certified organic, but often grown on very large farms and shipped across the country.

  3. 3
    Local and pastoral

    A meal from Polyface Farm in Virginia, where cattle, chickens and pigs rotate across grass pastures.

  4. 4
    Hunted and gathered

    A meal he made himself: a wild pig he hunted and mushrooms he foraged in California.

Same book, very different takeaways
Buy local and pasture-raised

Pollan’s own sympathies lie with small, diversified farms like Polyface.

Eat lower on the food chain

Others conclude that plant-rich diets cut land, water and emissions the most.

“

My hope is that we each take something away from this lecture, but every takeaway might be completely different.

12.1 · How Did Our Modern Agriculture Develop?

From Hunter-Gatherers to Agriculture

  1. Until ~10,000 years agoNomadic hunter-gatherers
  2. From ~10,500 years agoWheat, cattle and pigs in the Fertile Crescent; maize in Mexico ~9,000 years ago; chickens only ~3,500 years ago
  3. ~6,000 years agoIrrigation in Egypt and Mesopotamia; organic fertilizer from plant and animal waste in China
Foraging life
  • A varied diet
  • Fewer “work” hours
  • Violence
  • Predation
Farming life
  • Larger populations on less land
  • The gateway to cities, writing and modern society
  • Longer hours and a narrower diet
  • More disease

Books such as Sapiens and Guns, Germs, and Steel describe early farming as a hard, often miserable life, yet the road to the modern world.

Harari, Y. N. (2015). Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind. Harper.
Diamond, J. (1997). Guns, Germs, and Steel: The Fates of Human Societies. W. W. Norton.
Then and now

Farming once employed most workers. Today it employs a small share in richer countries.

Domestication
12.1 · Live

Where Did Our Food Come From?

True or false? Answer each one on your laptop. The instructor reveals them one at a time.

  1. 1
    Wild almonds are poisonous.

    Wild almond kernels make amygdalin, a bitter compound that releases cyanide. A mutation in a single gene switched it off, and early farmers kept the rare sweet trees.

    Sánchez-Pérez et al. (2019), “Mutation of a bHLH transcription factor allowed almond domestication,” Science 364:1095–1098.

  2. 2
    Wild bananas are packed with seeds.

    Bananas went from wild to edible through seed suppression and parthenocarpy: fruit that develops without seeds. Today’s bananas are sterile, so new plants are grown from shoots of old ones.

    Perrier et al. (2011), “Multidisciplinary perspectives on banana (Musa spp.) domestication,” PNAS 108:11311–11318; Heslop-Harrison & Schwarzacher (2007), Annals of Botany 100:1073–1084.

  3. 3
    There are over 4,000 edible varieties of potato.

    Most of them grow in the Andes of South America, the potato’s original home.

    International Potato Center (CIP), “Potato: facts and figures,” cipotato.org/potato.

  4. 4
    Broccoli, cabbage, kale, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts are all one species.

    All are Brassica oleracea, bred from one wild Mediterranean plant for different parts: leaves (kale, cabbage), flower buds (broccoli, cauliflower) and side buds (Brussels sprouts).

    Mabry et al. (2021), “The evolutionary history of wild, domesticated, and feral Brassica oleracea,” Molecular Biology and Evolution 38:4419–4434.

  5. 5
    Corn’s wild ancestor grew only about a dozen kernels per ear.

    Teosinte, a wild grass from Mexico, holds roughly ten to twelve kernels, each sealed in a stone-hard case. A change in one gene, tga1, helped expose the naked kernels we eat today.

    Doebley (2004), “The genetics of maize evolution,” Annual Review of Genetics 38:37–59; Wang et al. (2005), “The origin of the naked grains of maize,” Nature 436:714–719.

12.1 · Domestication

Selecting for Traits: How Humans Reshaped Our Food

For about 10,000 years, farmers saved the seeds and bred the animals with the traits they wanted. Small changes in each generation added up to foods their wild ancestors would not recognize.

1
Bigger ears, naked kernels
Teosinte → maize

About a dozen kernels sealed in stone-hard cases became hundreds of exposed ones.

2
Bigger fruit
Wild tomato → beefsteak

Fruit under 1 cm and a few grams became fruit of up to about a kilogram.

3
Smaller seeds
Wild banana → Cavendish

Hard seeds shrank to specks; farmed bananas are sterile and grown from shoots.

4
Grain that stays on
Wild wheat → bread wheat

Ears that scattered their ripe grain became ears that hold it until harvest.

5
Faster growth
1957 broiler → 2005 broiler

At 56 days on the same feed: 905 g vs. 4,202 g, more than 4 times heavier.

6
Different parts of one plant
Wild cabbage → six vegetables

Selecting for leaves, buds, flowers or stems turned one species into all six.

Sources: Doebley (2004), Annual Review of Genetics; Frary et al. (2000), Science; Perrier et al. (2011), PNAS; Fuller (2007), Annals of Botany; Zuidhof et al. (2014), Poultry Science; Mabry et al. (2021), Molecular Biology and Evolution.

Transportation
12.1 · Transportation and Refrigeration

Where Could You Buy a Banana?

How transportation and refrigeration changed what we eat

  1. 1
    By ship, to the ports

    For most of the 1800s, bananas arrived on ships and “they’d be sold at the port. But they weren’t generally commercially available anywhere.” By the 1890s they flooded into New York, Louisiana, Maryland, Pennsylvania and Alabama.

  2. 2
    Iced freight cars carry them inland

    Steamships and railroads changed that: freight cars with huge pieces of ice at each end. The Illinois Central reached New Orleans in 1882 and hauled bananas north to Chicago. Americans ate 15 million bunches in 1900 and 40 million by 1910.

  3. 3
    Refrigeration takes them everywhere

    Trains got mechanical refrigeration in the 1920s, then came refrigerated trucks in the 1930s. Bananas reached nearly every town.

  4. 4
    Pretend ASU is the port

    Imagine it is 1870 and the banana boat docks at ASU. Peddlers can carry the fruit about 3 miles across town before it bruises and overripens. Inside the circle you can buy a banana; outside, there are none.

  5. 5
    Where your banana runs out

    Tempe Marketplace (1.9 mi) and the Phoenix Zoo (2.1 mi): bananas. Old Town Scottsdale (4.8 mi), Sky Harbor Airport (4.9 mi), downtown Mesa (5.6 mi) and downtown Phoenix (8.6 mi): none. Until iced rail, that was life almost everywhere.

Then: V. S. Jenkins, Bananas: An American History (Smithsonian Institution Press, 2000), quoted from Freakonomics Radio; UC Santa Cruz Center for World History, “Modern History of the Banana”; Oxford American (2025) on Mobile; Encyclopedia of Chicago, “Illinois Central Railroad.” Pretend 1870: landmark distances are straight-line miles from ASU. Map boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau.

Synthetic Fertilizers and Pesticides
12.1 · Synthetic Fertilizer

Bread from Air: The Haber-Bosch Process

Every plant needs nitrogen, and the air is 78% nitrogen, but plants cannot use it: two nitrogen atoms hold each other with one of the strongest bonds in nature. For most of history, farmers relied on manure and legumes.

  1. 1840s
    Mining for nitrogen

    Farms ran short of nitrogen. Ships hauled seabird guano from Peru and saltpeter from Chile’s deserts to fertilize fields.

  2. 1898
    A warning

    Chemist William Crookes warned that the world’s wheat would fall short unless chemists could pull nitrogen from the air.

  3. 1909
    Haber’s breakthrough

    Fritz Haber made ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen on a lab bench, using high pressure, heat and a catalyst.

  4. 1913
    Bosch scales it up

    Carl Bosch turned the reaction into a factory at Oppau, Germany. Both men won Nobel Prizes (1918, 1931); Haber also led Germany’s World War I poison-gas program.

  5. Today
    Feeding half the world

    About 70% of ammonia becomes fertilizer. Synthetic nitrogen helps feed about half of humanity, and making it uses about 2% of the world’s energy.

Smil (2001), Enriching the Earth, MIT Press; Erisman et al. (2008), Nature Geoscience 1:636–639; IEA (2021), Ammonia Technology Roadmap; The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1918 and 1931, nobelprize.org.

12.1 · Synthetic Pesticides and Fertilizers

Two Agricultural Inputs with Outsized Environmental Consequences

Synthetic pesticides
87 of 115leading food crops

benefit from animal pollinators; some insecticides, such as neonicotinoids, can harm them.

Resistance

Overuse breeds resistant pests, so ever-stronger applications are needed over time.

10,000–20,000poisonings a year

diagnosed among about 2 million U.S. farmworkers (EPA/NIOSH).

Food chain

Persistent chemicals build up, harming predators above the insects they target.

Synthetic fertilizers
×10since 1961

Nitrogen fertilizer use: 11 million tonnes (1961) to 112 million tonnes (2023).

≈2%of the world’s energy

goes into making ammonia, mostly for fertilizer. The Haber-Bosch process runs largely on natural gas.

273×as potent as CO₂

Soil microbes turn some nitrogen into N₂O, a greenhouse gas (over 100 years).

Dead zones

Fertilizer runoff is the primary driver of eutrophication in rivers and coastal oceans.

Klein et al. (2007), Proc. R. Soc. B; EPA / NIOSH; IEA (2021), Ammonia Technology Roadmap; FAO via Our World in Data; IPCC AR6 (N₂O).

The Green Revolution
12.2 · The Green Revolution

The Price of Uniformity

A food system is the web of processes that connects farms to forks. The Green Revolution made that web far more productive, and far more uniform. Monocultures can yield more for a while, but they share the same weaknesses.

Three crops feed the world

Rice, maize and wheat provide nearly 60% of the calories and protein people get from plants.

Diversity lost

Since 1900, about 75% of crop genetic diversity has been lost as farmers swapped local varieties for uniform, high-yield ones.

One weakness, a whole field

In 1970, about 85% of U.S. corn shared one inherited trait. A new strain of leaf blight attacked it and destroyed about 15% of the crop.

FAO (2004), What Is Agrobiodiversity?; National Research Council (1972), Genetic Vulnerability of Major Crops; Ullstrup (1972), Annual Review of Phytopathology 10:37–50.

One Hectare of Wheat, Then and Now

The question

In 1961, one hectare of the world’s wheat fields grew enough grain for about 1,680 loaves of bread.

How many loaves does that same hectare grow today?

Class guesses 0

About 5,610 loaves, roughly 3.3 times as many. The world’s wheat yield rose from 1.09 to 3.64 tonnes per hectare. That is agricultural intensification: more output from the same land.

Wheat yield: FAO (2025), via Our World in Data, world averages for 1961 and 2024. Loaves: a 60-lb bushel of wheat makes about 42 commercial 1.5-lb loaves of white bread (Kansas Wheat).

12.2 · How Does Modern Agriculture Impact the Environment?

Agricultural Intensification and Its Costs

Farms grew more food on each hectare and spread across more land. Both reshaped the natural world.

1

Agricultural intensification means increasing agricultural output per unit of land. World cereal yields are about 3 times their 1961 level.

2

Agriculture has transformed ecosystems primarily by converting natural landscapes into cropland and pasture. Farms now cover half of the world’s habitable land; two-thirds of it is pasture.

3

Consequence: increased habitat loss and pollution. Clearing land is the top driver of biodiversity loss on land, and farm runoff pollutes rivers and coasts.

Cereal yield: FAO (2025), via Our World in Data. Land use: Our World in Data, “Land Use”; FAO (2023), Statistical Yearbook. Drivers of biodiversity loss: IPBES (2019), Global Assessment Report, Summary for Policymakers.

12.1 · The Green Revolution

The Green Revolution: More Grain from the Same Land

After 1960, a package of new tools spread across the world’s farms. Together they roughly tripled how much grain each hectare produces.

The toolkit
High-yield seeds

Norman Borlaug’s short-stalked wheat, bred in Mexico, spread to India and Pakistan in the 1960s. He won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize.

Synthetic fertilizer

Nitrogen pulled from the air by the Haber-Bosch process let fields carry far more grain.

Irrigation

Large-scale irrigation spread across the world’s farmland after 1960.

Synthetic pesticides

Chemical control of insects, weeds and fungi protected the new, denser crops.

Machinery

Gas and diesel engines replaced human and animal power: less labor, more fossil fuel.

And since the 1990s: genetic engineering. Today more than 90% of U.S. corn, soybean and cotton acres are genetically engineered varieties.

The payoff, world, 1961 to 2024

12.5 · How Have Our Food Systems Changed?

The Food-Water-Energy Nexus

The food-water-energy nexus is the interconnected relationship among food, water, and energy resources.

Water⇄Food

Farms take about 72% of the world’s freshwater withdrawals; fertilizer runoff returns as pollution.

Energy⇄Food

Food production often requires energy for machinery, transportation, and fertilizers. Food systems use about 30% of the world’s energy.

Water⇄Energy

Cooling power plants takes 41% of US water withdrawals, and moving water takes energy.

FAO AQUASTAT (2025); FAO, Energy-Smart Food for People and Climate (2011); USGS Fact Sheet 2018-3035 (2015 data).

12.5 · Food Insecurity

Food Security and Insecurity: Who Goes Without?

Food insecurity is a lack of secure access to enough safe, nutritious food. Food security is the reliable access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food.

Sustainable Food Systems
12.6 · How Do Our Food Choices Link to Sustainability?

Eating Lower on the Food Chain

Shepon et al. 2016; Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012; Poore & Nemecek 2018; USDA ERS; National Chicken Council; EPA. Full notes under “The same plate, side by side.”

The Same Plate, Side by Side

What it takes to put the same 1,000 Calories on your plate

Every plate holds the same 1,000 Calories. Beans and potatoes are eaten directly, so the Calories grown are the Calories eaten. A chicken turns about 13% of its feed Calories into food, and beef cattle about 3%, so 1,000 Calories of beef takes about 34,500 Calories of feed and about 10,200 liters of water: roughly 22 times the water of potatoes. Energy is lost at each step up the food chain.

Water: global average water footprint per Calorie, green + blue + grey (Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012, Ecosystems; beans = pulses, potatoes = starchy roots). Most of beef’s water is rain on pasture and feed crops. Feed: US feed-to-food Calorie conversion, beef 2.9% ± 0.7, poultry 13% ± 4 (Shepon et al. 2016, Environmental Research Letters); much of beef’s feed is pasture and hay that people cannot eat. Time on the farm: USDA ERS (cattle), National Chicken Council (broilers, 47 days), extension variety trials (beans, potatoes). Emissions: Poore & Nemecek (2018), Science, via Our World in Data; car miles at about 400 g CO₂ per mile (EPA).

12.6 · Organic, Fair Trade, and Local Food

Alternatives to Industrial Agriculture

Organic

Prohibits most synthetic pesticides and fertilizers (with set exceptions), GMOs and growth hormones; requires practices such as crop rotation. Certified by USDA-accredited agents.

Fair Trade

Certification standards, such as minimum prices and community premiums, aim to improve farmers’ and workers’ livelihoods and support sustainable production.

Buying Local / CSA

In Community Supported Agriculture, members buy a share of a local farm’s harvest in advance, supporting nearby farms and regional food systems.

Food miles and local food
1,640 kmabout 1,000 miles

Average final trip of U.S. food to the store (6,760 km across the whole supply chain).

Where U.S. food’s climate footprint comes from
Production 83%11%
transport (final delivery to stores: 4%)wholesale and retail
19%of food-system emissions

come from food miles worldwide. Fresh fruit and vegetables, kept cold, make over a third of that.

$9.0 billionsold locally, 2020

by more than 147,000 U.S. farms through farmers’ markets, farm stands, CSAs and local buyers.

The takeaway: what you eat usually matters more for the climate than how far it traveled, but buying local keeps money with nearby farms and cuts the energy of long, refrigerated trips.

Weber & Matthews (2008), Environmental Science & Technology 42:3508–3513; Li et al. (2022), Nature Food 3:445–453; USDA NASS (2022), 2020 Local Food Marketing Practices Survey.

12.6 · Reducing Food Waste and Restoring the Soil

Food Waste and Composting

Roughly one-third of the food produced for people is lost on farms and in supply chains or wasted in stores and homes (FAO, 2011). In the U.S., more is wasted in homes than in stores (USDA, 2010 data).

Every trip to the grocery store
Bring home 5 bags, and more than 1 bag’s worth goes uneaten.
23%of the food that reaches U.S. consumers is thrown away (2010)
$162Bof food wasted in U.S. stores and homes in 2010
1,249calories per person per day, uneaten
Where the scraps go
Landfill

Buried scraps rot without oxygen and release methane, about 80 times as potent as CO₂ over 20 years. Food is about 58% of the methane escaping U.S. landfills.

Compost

With oxygen, scraps break down into compost that returns nutrients and carbon to the soil.

USDA ERS: Buzby, Wells & Hyman (2014), EIB-121 (U.S., 2010; consumers wasted 90 of the 387 billion pounds that reached them); EPA (2023), Quantifying Methane Emissions from Landfilled Food Waste; IPCC AR6 (2021); FAO (2011), Global Food Losses and Food Waste.

Chapter 12 · Key Concepts

Food: How Do We Feed Ourselves?

Domestication
Saving the seeds and breeding the animals with the traits people want, generation after generation
Haber-Bosch Process
Making ammonia fertilizer from nitrogen in the air; synthetic nitrogen helps feed about half of humanity
Green Revolution
Post-1960 spread of high-yield seeds, synthetic inputs, irrigation and machinery that roughly tripled grain yields
Agrobiodiversity
The variety of crops and livestock; FAO estimates about 75% of crop genetic diversity was lost after 1900
Food-Water-Energy Nexus
The links among food, water and energy: producing one draws on the other two
Food Security
Reliable access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food
Organic Agriculture
Prohibits most synthetic pesticides and fertilizers (with exceptions), GMOs and hormones; requires crop rotation
Food Waste and Composting
Wasted food in landfills releases methane; composting turns scraps into nutrients for the soil
